## 1) Introduction

This script runs an ODE model for infectious disease case ascertainment, which simulates testing for, and the transmission dynamics of a healthcare-associated pathogen within a hospital setting. The model structure and parameters are specified to track the flow of patients through states of colonisation and infection with toxigenic *C. difficile*, to quantify the impact of testing on case detection, missed cases and consequent secondary cases among hospital patients.

The model does not simulate testing of symptomatic patients whose symptoms are not caused by *C. difficile*, or asymptomatic patients, so does not reflect all testing for CDI among hospital patients that occurs under real world conditions.

This report runs **Model 4**; earlier versions are listed in the model versions table in `README.md`.

To render this .qmd, either click on the 'Render' button above, or to render it with a date or other reference, type in the console:

`source("render_run.R")`\
`render_run("YYMMDD")`

This quarto document uses the ODE function defined in "Scripts/Model4_Functions.R" and the parameter sets defined in "Scripts/Model4_Parameters.R" to run a grid of scenarios, and generates and saves outputs in a labelled subdirectory of `Outputs/Model4/`.

Raw results from model runs are cached to avoid the need to re-run the full model if changes are made to the required outputs. The default set in this .qmd is to use cached results. The cache is re-used only if the scenario grid, fixed parameters, run settings, initial conditions and model functions are unchanged; if any of these change, the grid is re-run automatically. To force a re-run anyway, set `grid_clear_cache <- TRUE` in section [2) Initial setup].

### 1a) Model states and diagrams

The flow diagrams below are drawn from the model code each time this report is rendered (`Scripts/Model4_Diagrams.R`), so they always match the model. Each diagram's table of flows is first checked against the model's equations (`model_ode()`), and the render stops if they differ. The diagrams are saved as `flow_P1.png` to `flow_P3.png` in the run's output folder.

```{r}
#| label: flow-diagrams
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Draw the flow diagram for each isolation policy (section 2 starts by clearing the workspace, and
# section 3 sources the scripts again). Only the policy affects the diagram, so any daily probability of
# testing and sensitivity can be passed to make_mod_parms().
library(tidyverse)
library(deSolve)
source("Scripts/Model4_Functions.R")
source("Scripts/Model4_Parameters.R")
source("Scripts/Model4_Diagrams.R")
diagram_dir <- file.path("Outputs", "Model4", params$run_label)
dir.create(diagram_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
flow_diagrams <- tibble(
  code   = c("P1", "P2", "P3"),
  policy = c("none", "confirmed", "suspected_and_confirmed"),
  title  = c("P1: No isolation", "P2: Confirmed cases isolated", "P3: Suspected and confirmed cases isolated"),
  path   = file.path(diagram_dir, paste0("flow_", code, ".png"))
)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(flow_diagrams))) {
  parms <- make_mod_parms(flow_diagrams$policy[i], prob_test_daily = 0.03, test_sens = 0.5)
  check_model_flows(parms)
  save_flow_diagram(parms, flow_diagrams$path[i])
}
```

```{r}

  cat("![](", flow_diagrams$path[i], "){width=100%}\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

The main model compartments are:\
- **S (Susceptible)**: Not colonised or infected\
- **C (Colonised)**: Carrying the pathogen but not symptomatic\
- **I (Infected)**: Showing symptoms caused by the pathogen\
- **Xtest (Suspected cases)**: Symptomatic patients identified as suspected cases, being tested and awaiting test result\
- **FN (False negatives)**: Symptomatic patients with a false negative result, awaiting re-testing\
- **Xtreat (Confirmed cases)**: Symptomatic patients with a positive test result eceiving treatment, awaiting recovery and return to a general ward, or discharge\
- **D: Dead**: cumulative count of deaths (absorbing state)

How to read the diagrams:

- Each diagram shows only the states used under that isolation policy. States with a blue fill are in a side room/isolation bed, and the others are on a general ward. States with a dashed outline (T1 to T5) hold patients awaiting transfer between a general ward and a side room; see [1b) Alternative model structures].
- Patient states with a thick black outline are infectious; those with a grey outline are not.
- Arrows are labelled with the parameter that sets each flow, and the key box gives the formula for each rate from the input parameters. Grey arrows show discharges and deaths.
- A dot marks a forked arrow: patients leave a state at one rate (TIME) and are split between outcomes by proportions (PROPORTION). This applies to admissions, test results and the end of treatment.

Colonised patients and patients with CDI are infectious, and transmission is reduced if they are located in a side room/isolation bed:

- colonised patients (C) transmit at `betaC`, lower than for patients with CDI (by default 0.008 against 0.04);
- patients with CDI who are not yet on treatment (I, Xtest, FN, and T1, T3 and T4 awaiting transfer) transmit at `betaI` on a general ward, and at `betaI * beta_mult_isolated` in a side room/isolation bed;
- patients on treatment (Xtreat) are assumed to have waning infectiousness: they transmit at `betaXtreat` (the average over treatment, lower than `betaI`), times `beta_mult_isolated` in a side room, and are not infectious on exit from Xtreat;
- recovered patients awaiting transfer (T2, T5) and susceptible patients do not transmit.

Patient-to-patient transmission is frequency dependent: the colonisation rate of each susceptible patient is the sum of each infectious group's beta times its share of all patients in hospital. In addition, there is a background (environmental) colonisation rate, `beta0`, that applies to every susceptible patient and does not depend on the number of colonised or CDI patients in hospital. It reflects sources of acquisition other than current patients, such as visitors and staff, and the persistence of spores on surfaces.

The model does not include recovery from CDI without treatment: there is no flow from I (or Xtest or FN) back to C or S. Patients with CDI leave the infected states only by being treated (Xtreat), discharged or dying.

The duration and effectiveness of treatment are the same for CDI cases confirmed on their first test and for those confirmed after re-testing, having passed through FN. Patients with CDI do not clear the infection until treatment has been completed, so delays to treatment due to re-testing lengthen the duration of infection. The model does not capture any effect of these delays on CDI case severity or mortality, but it does quantify them: see the mean times from symptom onset to first test (Outcome D5) and to treatment (Outcome D6) in sections [13) Table of research question outcomes] and [14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity]. (Delays from moving patients to a side room under P2 and P3 are described in [1b) Alternative model structures].)

### 1b) Alternative model structures

There are three versions of the model with different structures that reflect different policies for isolation of suspected and confirmed CDI cases:\
- **P1:** No isolation of suspected or confirmed cases, patients remain on a general ward for testing and treatment;\
- **P2:** Isolation of confirmed cases: suspected cases remain on a general ward for testing and are moved to a side-room for treatment once a positive test result has confirmed CDI.\
- **P3:** Isolation of suspected and confirmed cases: symptomatic patients identified as suspected CDI cases are moved to a side-room for testing and remain there for treatment.

The model accounts for the time required to transfer patients between a general ward and a side room/isolation bed by creating patient transfer states T1 to T5. Patient transfer time is the time they remain in their original bed while the necessary arrangements are made. While infected patients remain on a general ward, they pose a higher risk of transmission than when they arrive in a side room. The time required for patient transfer will impact on the effectiveness of the isolation policy, and the isolation policy will modify the effect of test algorithm sensitivity on outcomes of interest, such as the number of hospital-acquired CDI cases.

The patient transfer states included in the model are: (see the transfer-state table in `README.md`):\
- **T1** (P2, general ward): confirmed case awaiting a side room for treatment (Xtest → T1 → Xtreat)\
- **T2** (P2, side room): recovered, awaiting return to a general ward (Xtreat → T2 → S)\
- **T3** (P3, general ward): suspected case awaiting a side room for testing (I or FN → T3 → Xtest)\
- **T4** (P3, side room): false negative awaiting return to a general ward (Xtest → T4 → FN)\
- **T5** (P3, side room): recovered, awaiting return to a general ward (Xtreat → T5 → S)

T1 and T3 transmit at `betaI` on a general ward, T4 at `betaI * beta_mult_isolated`, and T2 and T5 (recovered) not at all.

T1, T3 and T4 die at the infected rate, T2 and T5 at the baseline rate. Only T4 has discharges (at the FN rate).

The duration and effectiveness of treatment are the same in every version of the model (P1, P2 and P3). Patients with CDI do not clear the infection until treatment has been completed, so the delays from moving patients between a general ward and a side room under P2 and P3 lengthen the duration of infection: under P2, confirmed cases wait in T1 before starting treatment (a delay to treatment); under P3, suspected cases wait in T3 before the specimen is taken, and false negatives wait in T4 to return to the ward (delays to testing and so to treatment). The model does not capture any effect of these delays on CDI case severity or mortality, but it does quantify them: see the mean times from symptom onset to first test (Outcome D5) and to treatment (Outcome D6) in sections [13) Table of research question outcomes] and [14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity].

### 1c) Control variables

The control variables for scenarios are set as vectors in section [4) Set values for control variables], and every combination is run:\
- **isolation_policy**: P1 `"none"` (the reference policy), P2 `"confirmed"` or P3 `"suspected_and_confirmed"` (see [1b) Alternative model structures]).\
- **prob_test_daily**: Daily probability that an untested CDI case is sent for testing.\
- **test_sens**: Sensitivity of the diagnostic testing algorithm.

The model uses vectors of values for the daily probability of testing (`prob_test_daily`) and testing algorithm sensitivity (`test_sens`). The model presents results for each combination of control variables, as well as comparisons between isolation policies P2 and P3 with P1, and P3 with P2.

Test turnaround time (`t_test_turnaround`, 2.0 days) and patient transfer time (`t_patient_transfer`, 0.5 days) are fixed parameters in `Scripts/Model4_Parameters.R`, but could be set as control variables if different testing algorithms are expected to have different turnaround times, or to allow for longer delays in moving patients between a general ward and isolation in a side room.

**Daily probability of testing (`prob_test_daily`)**

`prob_test_daily` is the daily probability that an untested CDI case (in I) is identified as a suspected case and sent for testing. The model converts it to a daily rate, the case identification rate:

`gamma = -log(1 - prob_test_daily)` (`prob2rate(prob_test_daily, 1)`).

Patients move at rate `gamma` (a flow of `gamma * I`) from I to Xtest under P1 and P2, or from I to T3 under P3. No testing is `prob_test_daily = 0` (`gamma = 0`); `prob_test_daily` must be below 1, as `gamma` would be infinite at 1.

Identification competes with discharge and death from I, so these are outputs, not inputs (see the table in section [13) Table of research question outcomes]):

- the mean time to testing if not discharged or dead first: `1 / gamma`;
- the actual mean time to being sent for testing among the cases sent: `1 / (gamma + disI + mortI)`, shorter than `1 / gamma` because discharge and death cut off the longer waits;
- the share of incident CDI cases ever sent for testing: `gamma / (gamma + disI + mortI)`;
- the share of prevalent CDI cases ever tested at model stabilisation (Outcome A4): patient-days in Xtest, FN, Xtreat, T1, T4 and T3 from FN, out of patient-days in those states plus I and all of T3.

A point-prevalence study for hospital-onset diarrhoea (Mawer et al. 2019, doi 10.1016/j.jhin.2019.05.001) reports the share of hospital-onset diarrhoea (HOD) patients in hospital on the study day who had been tested for CDI during their hospital stay (75 of 230, 33%). This is a share of prevalent cases ever tested, comparable in kind with Outcome A4 for reference to real world evidence. However, its denominator is all HOD patients, not CDI cases, so it is not used to calibrate `prob_test_daily`.

**Testing algorithm sensitivity**

The model uses the test sensitivity (`test_sens`) and the test turnaround time to calculate two rates of exit from Xtest:\
- **confirmed case rate:** `theta = test_sens / t_test_turnaround` (to Xtreat; or under P2 to T1, awaiting a side room);\
- **false negative rate:** `pi = (1 - test_sens) / t_test_turnaround` (to FN; or under P3 to T4, awaiting return to the ward).

The share of results that are positive, `theta / (theta + pi)`, equals `test_sens` under every policy.

Because the model does not simulate testing of symptomatic patients that do not have CDI (or asymptomatic patients), there is no assumption for test algorithm specificity.

### 1d) Counting missed cases

Missed cases are patients with CDI that have not been tested (missed untested cases) or that have received a false negative test result (missed false negatives). Deaths while awaiting a test result (in Xtest) or treatment (in T1) are not counted as missed. It is assumed there are no discharges among patients while in Xtest, T1, T2, T3 or T5.

T3 is not split by origin, so deaths and tests in T3 are apportioned using the current flows into T3 from I and FN. This is exact at steady state, when the totals are counted.

Missed untested cases are counted as:\
- **P1 and P2:** deaths and discharges among patients in I;\
- **P3:** deaths and discharges among patients in I, plus deaths among patients while in T3 apportioned to flows from I to T3, i.e. multiplied by `gamma * I / (gamma * I + sigma * FN)`.

Missed false negatives are counted as:\
- **P1 and P2:** deaths and discharges among patients in FN;\
- **P3:** deaths and discharges among patients in FN and T4, plus deaths among patients while in T3 apportioned to flows from FN to T3, i.e. multiplied by `sigma * FN / (gamma * I + sigma * FN)`.

The share of infected patients identified as suspected cases (leaving I) is the same under every policy, so it is expected that under P3 (compared to P1 and P2) there will be slightly more missed untested cases due to deaths while in T3, and missed false negatives due to deaths and discharges while in T4.

### 1e) Counting tests and retests

It is assumed that the specimen is taken on entry into Xtest, so tests are counted as the flows into Xtest.

First tests are counted as:\
- **P1 and P2:** flows from I into Xtest;\
- **P3:** flows from T3 into Xtest apportioned to flows from I into T3, i.e. multiplied by `gamma * I / (gamma * I + sigma * FN)`.

Retests are counted as:\
- **P1 and P2:** flows from FN into Xtest;\
- **P3:** flows from T3 into Xtest apportioned to flows from FN into T3, i.e. multiplied by `sigma * FN / (gamma * I + sigma * FN)`.

### 1f) Model assumptions

Parameter values are fixed for the model run, e.g. there are no dynamic interactions between CDI case incidence and the daily probability of an untested case being tested, and no seasonal patterns in the proportions of admissions that are colonised or infected. The default values of the fixed parameters are set in `fixed` in `Scripts/Model4_Parameters.R`:

| Group | Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Admissions | `adm_rate` | 133 per day | Admissions per day (constant) |
|  | `prop_adm_C`, `prop_adm_I` | 8.6%, 0.2% | Share of admissions colonised (C) and infected (I); the rest are susceptible (S) |
| Length of stay (days) | `losS`, `losC` | 7, 7 | Mean length of stay of S and C (discharge rate = 1 / length of stay) |
|  | `losI`, `losFN` | 14, 14 | Mean length of stay of I and FN (the time actually spent in FN is shorter, as patients also leave by being retested) |
|  | `t_treatment` | 14 | Mean duration of treatment (Xtreat) |
|  | `prop_Xtreat_to_S` | 80% | Share of treated patients who return to a general ward as susceptible (the rest are discharged) |
| Mortality | `prob_mort_S` | 0.001 | Baseline risk of death over a stay of `losS` days (S and C, and recovered patients awaiting transfer, T2 and T5) |
|  | `mortI_mult` | 3 | Death rate of untreated CDI cases (I, Xtest, FN, and T1, T3 and T4) as a multiple of the baseline |
|  | `mortXtreat_mult` | 1.5 | Death rate of treated cases (Xtreat) as a multiple of the baseline |
| Transmission | `beta0` | 0.002 | Background (environmental) colonisation rate, independent of the number of colonised or CDI patients |
|  | `betaC` | 0.008 | Transmission from colonised patients (C) |
|  | `betaI` | 0.04 | Transmission from untreated CDI cases on a general ward (I, FN, Xtest under P1 and P2, T1, T3) |
|  | `betaXtreat` | 0.02 | Transmission from treated cases (Xtreat) on a general ward: the average over treatment, as shedding is assumed to fall from 0.04 at the start to 0 at the end |
|  | `beta_mult_isolated` | 0.05 | Multiplier on transmission for patients in a side room (Xtest under P3, T4, and Xtreat under P2 and P3) |
| Progression (C → I) | `prop_progress_C_to_I`, `t_progress_C_to_I` | 50%, 5 days | Share of colonised patients without antibiotics who progress to CDI, and mean time to progression |
|  | `abx_prop`, `abx_mult` | 37.3%, 2 | Share of colonised patients receiving antibiotics, and the relative risk of progression for them |
| Decolonisation (C → S) | `prop_decolonise_C_to_S`, `t_decolonise_C_to_S` | 5%, 5 days | Share of colonised patients who lose colonisation without treatment, and mean time to decolonisation |
| Testing and transfer (days) | `t_test_turnaround` | 2 | Mean time from specimen collection to test result |
|  | `t_wait_retest` | 7 | Mean time from a false negative result to retest |
|  | `t_patient_transfer` | 0.5 | Mean time to move a patient between a general ward and a side room |

The control variables (isolation policy, daily probability of testing and test sensitivity) are set in [4) Set values for control variables]. Every time is exponentially distributed (constant rates), with the mean shown.

**Pathogen and population**

- A single toxigenic strain is in circulation.
- The hospital is a single, well-mixed population: there are no separate wards or bays. The model is deterministic and its parameters don't change over time (no seasonality or change in testing practice due to changes in CDI incidence).
- Patients are not followed after discharge. Readmission and transmission in the community are not modelled.

**Admissions, discharges and deaths**

- Admissions arrive at a constant rate. They do not replace discharges, so the hospital census can vary.
- Admissions are split between S, C and I in fixed proportions reflecting community prevalence, which is not affected by discharges from the hospital. Nobody is admitted directly to Xtest or Xtreat.
- Each state has its own constant discharge rate, set by its length of stay. Patients awaiting a test result (Xtest) stay in hospital until the result arrives, and patients awaiting transfer can't be discharged, except false negatives awaiting return to the ward (T4), who are discharged at the FN rate.
- Treated patients either return to a general ward as susceptible or are discharged. If isolated (P2 and P3), those returning to the ward wait in T2 or T5 for transfer.
- Death rates are constant, and higher for CDI cases than for other patients (see the table).

**Colonisation and progression**

- Susceptible patients become colonised through background (environmental) acquisition, which doesn't depend on the number of patients in each state, and frequency-dependent transmission from colonised and infected patients: λ = β₀ + Σβₖk/N (see [1a) Model states and diagrams]).
- Isolation in a side room reduces transmission (by `beta_mult_isolated`); it does not eliminate it. Patients awaiting transfer transmit as untreated CDI cases in their current bed; recovered patients (T2, T5) don't transmit.
- Progression from C to I is increased by antibiotic exposure among colonised patients (SCI structure, not PSCIX).
- Colonised patients can lose colonisation without treatment, but there is no recovery from infection (state I) without treatment.
- There is no immunity, and no recurrence or relapse. Patients who recover after treatment return to the susceptible state.
- Colonised patients are not screened, detected or decolonised.

**Case identification and testing**

- Only infected (symptomatic) patients are identified as suspected cases and tested. Patients in S and C don't develop diarrhoea that leads to testing. As a result, "faecal specimens tested" counts only tests of patients with CDI, and underestimates real world testing volume.
- The daily probability that an untested CDI case is sent for testing (`prob_test_daily`) sets a constant identification rate, `-log(1 - prob_test_daily)`. Every untested case has the same chance of being identified each day regardless of time since onset of CDI, competing with discharge and death, so the share of cases ever tested and the actual mean time to testing among cases tested both follow from it (see [1c) Control variables]).
- The specimen is collected on entry to Xtest, and treatment starts on entry to Xtreat. Patients waiting for transfer are not yet tested or treated: under P3, suspected cases waiting in T3 for a side room have not yet had a specimen collected (and false negatives waiting in T3 have not yet been retested); under P2, confirmed cases waiting in T1 for a side room have not yet started treatment. So under P2 and P3 the transfer time adds to the time to testing and/or treatment (see [1b) Alternative model structures]).
- Each test, including retests, returns a positive result with probability equal to the test sensitivity. Results of repeat tests on the same patient are independent.
- Patients with a false-negative result return to a general ward (FN), still symptomatic and transmitting, and are retested unless they are discharged or die first.
- Confirmed cases are treated. Under P2 and P3 they are isolated; under P1 they stay on a general ward.
- Patients wait for a move between a general ward and a side room in a transfer state (T1-T5) in their original bed, and leave it at rate `tau = 1 / t_patient_transfer`.
- Side-room capacity is unlimited.

**Treatment and recovery**

- Treatment for confirmed cases is started on entry to Xtreat.
- Patients remain in Xtreat for the mean duration of treatment (`t_treatment`), which allows for treatment, recovery and a symptom-free period to ensure patients are not infectious on exit from Xtreat.
- Treatment always works: every treated patient who does not die recovers. There is no treatment failure, and treatment clears colonisation as well as infection, so recovered patients return to S, not C.
- As for the other times in the model, the time in Xtreat is exponentially distributed with mean `t_treatment`, so some patients leave sooner and some later.
- Patients are not discharged part-way through treatment. At the end of treatment, a proportion of recovered patients (`prop_Xtreat_to_S`) remain in hospital for treatment of other conditions, and the remainder are discharged from hospital (a single exit rate, 1 / `t_treatment`, split by `prop_Xtreat_to_S`: the forked arrow in the diagrams in [1a) Model states and diagrams]).
- Patients who remain in hospital return to a general ward (via T2 or T5 under P2 and P3) as ordinary susceptible patients: they are discharged at the S rate (`losS`) and can be colonised again.
- Treated patients die at `mortXtreat_mult` times the baseline death rate, lower than for untreated CDI cases (`mortI_mult`).

### 1g) Research questions and outcomes of interest

The model quantifies the impact of testing on CDI case ascertainment; transmission of *C. difficile* (and consequent colonisations and infections); hospital resource use and CDI case outcomes.

**CDI case definitions**

- **Hospital-onset CDI:** all in-hospital C→I progressions, i.e. patients admitted colonised plus patients colonised in hospital who progress to CDI during their stay.
- **Hospital-acquired CDI:** in-hospital C→I progressions, multiplied by the share of all colonisations that were acquired in hospital (a subset of hospital-onset CDI). This assumes patients colonised in hospital and those admitted colonised progress at the same rate.

Differences in total and hospital-onset CDI cases between scenarios are driven entirely by differences in hospital-acquired CDI, because admissions and the prevalence of colonisation and CDI among admitted patients are fixed (see [1f) Model assumptions]), and testing and isolation affect only infected patients.

**Outcomes of interest**

Each outcome is evaluated across the full range of the control variables (every combination of isolation policy, daily probability of testing and test sensitivity in the scenario grid): see the plots in section [14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity]. The outcomes are also compared for an improvement in test sensitivity from 50% to 80%, for P1, P2 and P3, across the range of the daily probability of testing (plots in section [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity]) and in tables at a daily probability of testing of 0.03 and 0.40 (section [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity]). The research question outcomes table (section [13) Table of research question outcomes]) shows every outcome for the example scenarios.

Where outcomes are described as estimates, they are calculated using the shares of patient flows from one state to multiple states, or from multiple states to one state: hospital-acquired CDI as in the definition above, and cases confirmed through re-testing by apportioning the flow from Xtest to Xtreat by the share of flows into Xtest that are retests (from FN) rather than first tests (from I; see [1e) Counting tests and retests]).

**A) Case ascertainment:**

1)  the total number of incident CDI cases (to include patients that were colonised on admission that progress to CDI during their hospital stay, patients admitted with CDI and patients that become colonised and progress to CDI during their hospital stay);
2)  the number of missed CDI cases, untested or after a false negative result (counted as described in [1d) Counting missed cases]);
3)  the proportion of incident CDI cases that are ever sent for testing (see [1c) Control variables]);
4)  the proportion of CDI cases in hospital that have ever been tested for CDI, as a point prevalence at model stabilisation (see [1c) Control variables]);
5)  the number and proportion of incident CDI cases amongst hospital patients that are confirmed through diagnostic testing;
6)  the estimated number and proportion of incident CDI cases that are confirmed through re-testing following a false-negative test result (delayed diagnosis).

**B) Transmission of *C. difficile*:**

1)  the estimated number of hospital-acquired colonisations (patients that become colonised during their hospital stay); and
2)  the estimated number of hospital-acquired infections (patients that become colonised and progress to CDI during their hospital stay); and
3)  the prevalence of colonisation and infection amongst discharged patients, and its difference from the prevalence amongst admitted patients.

**C) Hospital resource use:**

1)  total hospital bed occupancy (patient bed-days), reflecting any impacts on bed pressure, and average patient length of stay;
2)  general ward bed occupancy;
3)  required side room bed occupancy;
4)  the proportion of hospital bed occupancy that is required for patient isolation in a side room;
5)  the number of faecal specimens collected and tested for CDI (first tests and retests, as counted in [1e) Counting tests and retests]);
6)  the number of faecal specimens collected and tested for CDI per CDI case confirmed;
7)  the number of confirmed cases that are started on treatment for CDI (equal to Outcome A5).

**D) CDI case outcomes:**

1)  the number of incident CDI cases that are treated and recover (then either returned to a general ward or discharged);
2)  the number of incident CDI cases that are discharged untreated;
3)  the number of incident CDI cases that die in hospital (with no specimen sent for testing, awaiting a test result, awaiting re-testing following a false negative test result, or during treatment);
4)  number of CDI-attributable deaths in hospital (accounting for deaths that may have occurred due to other causes);
5)  the mean time from CDI symptom onset to first test (when the specimen is taken), among the cases tested;
6)  the mean time from CDI symptom onset to the start of treatment, among the cases treated (including delays from re-testing and from transfer to a side room; see [1a) Model states and diagrams] and [1b) Alternative model structures]).

**Outputs required for cost effectiveness analysis (CEA) or cost utility analysis (CUA)**

CEA involves calculation of Incremental Cost Effectiveness Ratios (ICERs) for specific changes in testing or isolation policy, that allows comparison of multiple outcomes within a single metric, cost per avoided hospital-acquired CDI case. For cost-utility analysis the metric is £ cost per avoided QALY loss. CEA and CUA would require information on the hospital resource costs (specimen collection and testing, side room and general ward patient care, CDI treatment). CUA would require patient welfare values for untreated, treated/recovered CDI cases and deaths from CDI (discounted QALY losses).

The CEA/CUA would not take account of outcomes for CDI cases that occur in the community, as a result of:

- discharged colonisations that progress to infection;
- onwards transmission from discharged colonised or infected patients.

Model outcomes required for calculation of an ICER for a change in testing or isolation are shown in the tables below. The model does not include parameter values for costs of general ward and side-room patient care, CDI testing and treatment or QALY losses due to CDI morbidity or mortality, so does not calculate ICERs.

**ICER numerator, change in costs**

| Model outcome | ICER numerator |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Number of patient days on a general ward | × general ward care, cost per day |
| Number of patient days in a side room | × side room care, cost per day |
| Number of confirmed CDI cases | × CDI antimicrobial therapy, cost per course of treatment |
| Number of faecal specimens tested for CDI | × specimen collection and testing, cost per specimen |

**ICER denominator, avoided hospital-acquired CDI case**

| Model outcome                         | ICER denominator |
|---------------------------------------|------------------|
| Number of hospital-acquired CDI cases |                  |

**ICER denominator, avoided QALY loss**

| Model outcome                          | ICER denominator                  |
|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| Number of treated, recovered CDI cases | × QALY loss for treated cases     |
| Number of untreated, discharged cases  | × QALY loss for untreated cases   |
| Number of CDI-attributable deaths      | × discounted QALY loss for deaths |

Extending the model to include probabilistic analysis, with distributions for uncertain parameters would allow value of information analysis.

### 1h) Potential model developments

**Specimen collection and start of treatment while awaiting transfer (P2 and P3).** At present the specimen is collected on entry to Xtest and treatment starts on entry to Xtreat, so under P3 suspected cases waiting in T3 for a side room are not yet tested, and under P2 confirmed cases waiting in T1 are not yet treated (see [1f) Model assumptions]). In practice the specimen could be collected as soon as a case is suspected, and treatment started as soon as it is confirmed, while the move to a side room is arranged. To model this:

- P3: count the test on entry to T3 (so deaths in T3 of patients from I would be tested cases, not missed untested cases), and shorten the mean time in Xtest to the test turnaround time minus the patient transfer time (`theta` and `pi` set from `t_test_turnaround - t_patient_transfer`), so the mean time from specimen to result is unchanged;
- P2: start treatment on entry to T1 (T1 patients would transmit at `betaXtreat` on a general ward, and die at the treated rate), and shorten the mean time in Xtreat to the mean duration of treatment minus the patient transfer time (`t_treatment - t_patient_transfer`), so the mean duration of treatment is unchanged;
- this needs the turnaround time and the duration of treatment to be longer than the transfer time. With exponentially distributed times, the means are preserved but a result could still arrive before an individual patient's move; and the mean times to first test and to treatment (Outcomes D5, D6) would no longer include the transfer time.

The transfer would then affect where patients are cared for (and so transmission), but no longer delay testing or treatment.

**Environmental contamination that varies with prevalence.** At present background (environmental) acquisition is a constant rate, `beta0`, that does not depend on the number of colonised or CDI patients in hospital (see [1a) Model states and diagrams]). It could instead be linked to them through a stock of *C. difficile* spores in the environment, a new state "Env":

- spores enter Env in proportion to the patient bed-days in each infectious state (C to Xtreat, and T1, T3 and T4), at a lower rate for C and Xtreat, and for patients isolated in a side room;
- spores leave Env at rate 1 / (mean duration of spore persistence), e.g. 180 days, so `dEnv/dt = sum(shedding rate × patients in each state) - Env / 180`;
- the background colonisation rate then varies with the size of Env, e.g. `beta0 = beta_env × Env`, possibly plus a constant for sources not linked to current patients (visitors and staff).

This would give a relationship between environmental contamination and the prevalence of colonisation and CDI, with a lag: environmental exposure would build up and decline over months after a change in testing or isolation, so the burn-in would need to be longer than a few multiples of the persistence time. It could be difficult to parameterise: shedding rates by state and location, spore persistence (and the effect of cleaning) and the relationship between contamination and acquisition are uncertain. One option is to choose `beta_env` so that the baseline scenario reproduces the current `beta0`.

**Other possible developments:**

- testing of patients with diarrhoea not caused by *C. difficile* and of colonised patients, with a control variable for test specificity to quantify false positives, so that testing volume and treatment of non-CDI cases better reflect real-world conditions and consequences for hospital resource use. For this, it would be necessary to set an assumption or draw from evidence on the prevalence of admitted patients with non-CDI diarrhoeal symptoms, and the incidence of non-CDI hospital onset diarrhoea (HOD). For example, the HOD prevalence observed in Mawer, et al. (2019) could be used to set an assumption for overall HOD incidence (including CDI-related HOD), given as assumptions for the mean length of stay for the study population and mean duration of HOD symptoms;
- limited side-room capacity, so that isolation depends on availability;
- recurrence or relapse of CDI after treatment, and readmission of discharged patients;
- non-exponential times (e.g. a test turnaround made of several stages, so that turnaround times are less variable);
- parameter values that change over time (e.g. to reflect seasonal patterns in admissions and proportion of admissions that are colonised or infected on admission);
- parameter values that change in response to rising incidence (e.g. increasing the probability of an untested case being tested if incidence rates go above a specified level, to simulate an outbreak response);
- a daily probability of testing an untested case that depends on time since onset of CDI;
- probabilistic analysis, with distributions for uncertain parameters rather than point values or vectors; and
- transmission, colonisation and infection in the community.

## 2) Initial setup

Load libraries, set options, and create an output directory for this run.

The grid results from running the model ([7) Run scenarios]) are cached in `grid_runs.rds` in the output folder. If `grid_clear_cache <- FALSE`, they are re-used on the next render if the scenario grid, fixed parameters, run settings, initial conditions and the model, parameter, validation, grid-running and post-processing functions are unchanged; otherwise the grid is re-run. Set `grid_clear_cache <- TRUE` to force a re-run.

```{r}
#| label: initial-setup
 
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), "params"))
library(tidyverse)
library(deSolve)
library(scales)
library(cowplot)
library(dplyr)
options(scipen = 1000)
output_dir <- file.path("Outputs", "Model4", params$run_label)
dir.create(output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

grid_clear_cache <- FALSE
```

## 3) Source parameters and functions

Source the ODE functions and parameter sets for the model. The functions include the ODE system definition, scenario running functions, and various post-processing functions for summarising and plotting results. The parameters script defines the fixed model parameters (e.g., transmission rates, recovery rates, test turnaround time) and the `make_mod_parms()` function used to build each scenario's parameter list.

```{r}
#| label: source-parameters-and-functions

source("Scripts/Model4_Functions.R")
source("Scripts/Model4_Parameters.R")
```

## 4) Set values for control variables

Set the values of each control variable as a vector. Every combination of isolation policy, daily probability of testing and test sensitivity is run (the scenario grid). Scenario labels combine a policy code (`P1_none`, `P2_confirmed`, `P3_susp_conf`) with the daily probability of testing and the sensitivity as whole percentages, e.g. `P2_confirmed_test007_sens100` (`test000` is no testing), so both must be multiples of 0.01. The daily probabilities are unevenly spaced, with more values at the low end, where outcomes change fastest; they cover a mean time to testing if not discharged or dead first of about 100 days (0.01) to 2 days (0.40), plus no testing (0.00).

A small set of example scenarios is taken from the grid for the time-series plots, annual summaries and outcome tables (sections [10) Time-series plots up to stabilisation] to [13) Table of research question outcomes]): each isolation policy at each setting of daily probability of testing and sensitivity in `example_settings`, in the order listed (by default 0.03 and 0.40, about 33 and 2 days' mean time to testing if not discharged or dead first, each at 50% and 100% sensitivity; 12 scenarios).

```{r}
#| label: set-values-for-control-variable-values

# Control variables: every combination is run
isolation_policy <- c("none", "confirmed", "suspected_and_confirmed")   # P1, P2, P3
# Daily probability that an untested CDI case is sent for testing (multiples of 0.01, must be < 1;
# 0 = no testing). gamma = -log(1 - prob_test_daily)
prob_test_daily  <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40) / 100
test_sens        <- seq(0, 100, by = 10) / 100

scenario_grid <- make_scenario_grid(isolation_policy, prob_test_daily, test_sens)

# Example settings, in the order shown in sections 10 and 12 (must be values in the vectors above)
example_settings <- tribble(
  ~prob_test_daily, ~test_sens,
  0.03,             0.5,
  0.40,             0.5,
  0.03,             1,
  0.40,             1
)

example_grid <- scenario_grid |>
  semi_join(example_settings, by = c("prob_test_daily", "test_sens"))
if (nrow(example_grid) != length(isolation_policy) * nrow(example_settings)) {
  stop("Some example settings are not in the grid: check example_settings against the vectors above.")
}

control_parms <- scenario_grid |>
  mutate(t_test_turnaround = fixed$t_test_turnaround)
write_csv(control_parms,
          file.path(output_dir, "scenario_control_parameters.csv"))

cat("Scenario grid:", nrow(scenario_grid), "scenarios (",
    length(isolation_policy), "policies x", length(prob_test_daily), "daily probabilities of testing (including no testing) x",
    length(test_sens), "sensitivity values). Example scenarios:", nrow(example_grid), "\n")
```

## 5) Model settings

Set the total model run time, the time step for the ODE solver and the burn-in period. The burn-in is the period at the start of the run while the model moves from its initial conditions to steady state; it is excluded from all cumulative totals, patient-days and annual summaries, which cover the analysis period after it. The burn-in is the same for every scenario, so all totals cover the same length of time (here a 1-year burn-in and a 5-year analysis period, in a 6-year run). Sections [12) Plots of annual summaries] to [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity] show annual totals (the analysis-period total divided by its length in years), for comparison with surveillance data. Section [9) Stabilisation summary] checks that every scenario has stabilised before the end of the burn-in, and stops the render if not. Validate that the settings are appropriate (all positive, the time step smaller than the model time, and the burn-in shorter than the model time). Create a sequence of time points for the model output.

```{r}
#| label: model-settings

run_settings <- list(
  model_time = 365 * 6,
  time_step  = 0.5,
  burn_in    = 365
)
validate_run_settings(run_settings$model_time, run_settings$time_step, run_settings$burn_in)
model_time <- run_settings$model_time
time_step  <- run_settings$time_step
burn_in    <- run_settings$burn_in
analysis_years <- (model_time - burn_in) / 365
mod.t      <- seq(0, model_time, by = time_step)
```

## 6) Initial conditions

Set the initial conditions for the model states (S, C, I, Xtest, FN, Xtreat, the transfer states T1-T5, and D) at time 0. These values represent the starting point of the simulation and can be adjusted as needed for different scenarios or sensitivity analyses. The order must match the order of the derivatives returned by the ODE function (`model_ode()` in `Scripts/Model4_Functions.R`).

```{r}
#| label: initial-conditions

S0      <- 909
C0      <- 86
I0      <- 5
Xtest0  <- 0
FN0     <- 0
Xtreat0 <- 0
T10     <- 0
T20     <- 0
T30     <- 0
T40     <- 0
T50     <- 0
D0      <- 0
mod.init <- c(
  S      = S0,
  C      = C0,
  I      = I0,
  Xtest  = Xtest0,
  FN     = FN0,
  Xtreat = Xtreat0,
  T1     = T10,
  T2     = T20,
  T3     = T30,
  T4     = T40,
  T5     = T50,
  D      = D0
)
```

## 7) Run scenarios

Run the ODE model for every scenario in the grid using `run_scenario_grid()`. Each run is post-processed with `add_quantities()`, which multiplies each output row by the time step to give per-step flows and patient-days (rows in the burn-in, including time 0, are given zero width, so cumulative totals cover exactly the analysis period after the burn-in), and immediately summarised (parameters, final cumulative outcomes, patient-days, stabilisation and any negative values), so full time series are not kept for the whole grid.

The grid results are cached in `grid_runs.rds` in the output folder. They are re-used on the next render if the scenario grid, fixed parameters, run settings, initial conditions and the model, parameter, validation, grid-running and post-processing functions are unchanged; otherwise the grid is re-run. Set `grid_clear_cache <- TRUE` in the setup section [2) Initial setup] to force a re-run, or FALSE to use the cached grid results.

The grid runs in parallel on `grid_n_cores` CPU cores (default: all physical cores but one); set it to 1 to run one scenario at a time in this session.

The example scenarios are then re-run to keep their full time series, which are saved as `solution_<scenario>.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: run-scenarios

grid_cache_file  <- file.path(output_dir, "grid_runs.rds")

# Number of CPU cores used to run the grid in parallel (1 = run in this session, one at a time)
grid_n_cores <- max(1, parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE) - 1)

grid_cache_key <- list(
  scenario_grid = scenario_grid,
  fixed         = fixed,
  run_settings  = run_settings,
  mod.init      = mod.init,
  code          = lapply(list(model_ode, make_mod_parms, prob2rate, validate_fixed_parameters,
                              validate_scenario_inputs, validate_rate_parameters, run_scenario,
                              run_scenario_grid, add_quantities, make_final_outcomes,
                              calculate_total_patient_days, stabilisation_summary,
                              find_stabilisation_day, negative_value_rows, mean_wait_to_state), deparse)
)

grid_cache <- if (!grid_clear_cache && file.exists(grid_cache_file)) readRDS(grid_cache_file) else NULL

if (!is.null(grid_cache) && identical(grid_cache$key, grid_cache_key)) {
  grid_runs <- grid_cache$runs
  cat("Loaded scenario grid results from", grid_cache_file, "\n")
} else {
  grid_runs <- run_scenario_grid(scenario_grid, time_step, burn_in = burn_in, n_cores = grid_n_cores)
  saveRDS(list(key = grid_cache_key, runs = grid_runs), grid_cache_file)
  cat("Ran", nrow(scenario_grid), "scenarios and saved results to", grid_cache_file, "\n")
}

# One row per scenario: control values, final cumulative outcomes and patient-days
grid_results <- make_grid_results(scenario_grid, grid_runs)

# Annual totals: every count and patient-day column divided by the length of the analysis period
grid_results_annual <- grid_results |>
  mutate(across(c(starts_with("cum_"), ends_with("_days")), \(x) x / analysis_years))

# Long format for the outcomes compared across the grid (sections 14 and 15), as annual totals, and
# differences between policies (P2 vs P1, P3 vs P1, P3 vs P2)
grid_long  <- make_grid_outcomes_long(grid_results, years = analysis_years)
grid_diffs <- make_grid_diffs(grid_long)

write_csv(grid_runs$parms,
          file.path(output_dir, "model_parameters_all_scenarios.csv"))
write_csv(grid_runs$patient_days, file.path(output_dir, "patient_days_summary.csv"))

# Example scenarios: re-run and keep full time series
example_parms <- pmap(example_grid, \(scenario, isolation_policy, prob_test_daily, test_sens)
  make_mod_parms(isolation_policy = isolation_policy,
                 prob_test_daily = prob_test_daily,
                 test_sens        = test_sens,
                 scenario_label   = scenario)) |>
  set_names(example_grid$scenario)

scenario_post <- lapply(example_parms, \(p) run_scenario(p) |> add_quantities(time_step = time_step, burn_in = burn_in))

walk2(scenario_post,
      names(scenario_post),
      ~ write_csv(.x, file.path(
        output_dir, paste0("solution_", .y, ".csv")
      )))

# Patient-days for the example scenarios (all scenarios are saved in patient_days_summary.csv;
# section 13 shows them per year)
patient_days_summary <- grid_runs$patient_days |>
  filter(scenario %in% example_grid$scenario)
```

## 8) Negative values checks

Check for any negative values in the model states or flows, which may indicate numerical issues with the ODE solver or problems with the model structure. The `negative_value_rows` function identifies rows in the data frame where any state or flow has a negative value. This is checked for every scenario in the grid, and all negative rows are saved to one CSV for further investigation.

```{r}
#| label: negative_values_check

neg_combined <- grid_runs$negatives

# Output to screen
if (nrow(neg_combined) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(count(neg_combined, scenario, name = "negative_rows"),
               caption = "Scenarios with negative model output rows")
} else {
  cat("No negative values found in any of the", nrow(scenario_grid), "scenarios.\n")
}

# Save as CSV
write_csv(neg_combined, file.path(output_dir, "all_negative_rows_combined.csv"))
```

## 9) Stabilisation summary

Identify the day on which the model states stabilise for every scenario in the grid using the `stabilisation_summary` function. This function determines when the values of the states reach a steady state (i.e., change by less than a tolerance of 1e-4 per time step for a specified number of consecutive time steps). Note that the `consecutive_days` setting and output column count time steps, not days: the default of 10 is 10 half-day steps, i.e. 5 days. The full summary for all scenarios is saved as a CSV; the table shows the example scenarios.

**The burn-in (section [5) Model settings]) must be longer than the stabilisation period of every scenario, so that the totals cover steady-state behaviour only.** The code below checks whether any scenario has not stabilised by the end of the burn-in, the render stops with an error listing those scenarios, and `burn_in` (and `model_time`) should be increased. The longest stabilisation period across the example scenarios sets the time window for the time-series plots in section [10) Time-series plots up to stabilisation], which therefore show the approach to steady state during the burn-in.

```{r}
#| label: stabilisation-summary

stability_all <- grid_runs$stability
write_csv(stability_all,
          file.path(output_dir, "stabilisation_summary_states_flows.csv"))

not_stabilised <- stability_all |> filter(!stabilised) |> pull(scenario)
cat(sum(stability_all$stabilised), "of", nrow(stability_all),
    "scenarios stabilised; latest stabilisation day across the grid:",
    max(stability_all$stabilisation_day, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
if (length(not_stabilised) > 0) {
  cat("Not stabilised within the run:", paste(not_stabilised, collapse = ", "), "\n")
}

# Check the burn-in is longer than the stabilisation period of every scenario; stop if not
late_stabilisation <- stability_all |>
  filter(!stabilised | stabilisation_day >= burn_in) |>
  pull(scenario)
if (length(late_stabilisation) > 0) {
  stop(length(late_stabilisation), " scenario(s) did not stabilise before the end of the ",
       burn_in, "-day burn-in: ", paste(late_stabilisation, collapse = ", "),
       ". Increase burn_in (and model_time) in section 5.")
}
cat("All scenarios stabilised before the end of the ", burn_in, "-day burn-in (latest: day ",
    max(stability_all$stabilisation_day), ").\n", sep = "")

stability_examples <- stability_all |> filter(scenario %in% example_grid$scenario)
longest_stabilisation <- max(stability_examples$stabilisation_day, na.rm = TRUE)
knitr::kable(stability_examples, caption = "Stabilisation: model states and flows, example scenarios")
```

## 10) Time-series plots up to stabilisation

Sections [10) Time-series plots up to stabilisation] to [12) Plots of annual summaries] show results for the example scenarios that help verify the model is working as expected; sections [13) Table of research question outcomes] to [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity] present the results for the write-up.

Plot the model states and flows over time for the example scenarios, from the start of the run up to the longest stabilisation period across the example scenarios (section [9) Stabilisation summary]), i.e. the approach to steady state during the burn-in. The plots show each isolation policy in a column (P1, P2, P3) and each setting of daily probability of testing and sensitivity in a row, in the order set in `example_settings` (section [4) Set values for control variables]). Each plot is saved as a PNG file in the output directory and shown in a tab.

```{r}
#| label: time-series-plots-save

final_outcomes         <- grid_runs$final
example_final_outcomes <- final_outcomes |> filter(scenario %in% example_grid$scenario)

# Annual totals: counts and patient-days divided by the length of the analysis period
annualise <- \(df) df |> mutate(across(c(starts_with("cum_"), ends_with("_days")), \(x) x / analysis_years))

example_annual_outcomes <- annualise(example_final_outcomes)
example_annual_bed_days <- annualise(patient_days_summary)

# Generate input data for plots
plot_long_states        <- make_plot_long_states(scenario_post, longest_stabilisation)
plot_long_bed_occupancy <- make_plot_long_bed_occupancy(scenario_post, longest_stabilisation)
plot_long_flows         <- make_plot_long_flows(scenario_post)

# Plots, in display order: file name (without .png), tab title, plot and size (cm), with one row of
# panels per setting. Every plot in the report is saved 24 cm wide and shown at the page width, so text
# (font_base_size) appears the same size in every section.
ts_width  <- 24
ts_height <- 8 + 5 * nrow(example_settings)
time_series_plots <- tribble(
  ~file,                               ~title,                              ~plot,                                                                                 ~width,   ~height,
  "plot_states_lines_facet",           "States",                            plot_states_line(plot_long_states),                                                    ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_states_lines_facet_noS",       "States (excluding S)",              plot_states_line_noS(plot_long_states),                                                ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_states_area_facet",            "States (area)",                     plot_states_area(plot_long_states),                                                    ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_states_area_facet_noS",        "States (area, excluding S)",        plot_states_area_noS(plot_long_states),                                                ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_bed_occupancy",                "Bed occupancy",                     plot_bed_occupancy(plot_long_bed_occupancy, longest_stabilisation),                   ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_flows_to_C_and_I",             "New colonisations and infections",  plot_flows_to_C_and_I(plot_long_flows, longest_stabilisation, example_final_outcomes), ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_case_ascertainment_line",      "Case ascertainment",                plot_case_ascertainment_line(plot_long_flows, longest_stabilisation),                  ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_deaths_by_state_area_noS",     "Deaths by state",                   plot_deaths_by_state_area_noS(plot_long_flows, longest_stabilisation),                 ts_width, ts_height,
  "plot_discharges_by_state_area_noS", "Discharges by state",               plot_discharges_by_state_area_noS(plot_long_flows, longest_stabilisation),             ts_width, ts_height
) |>
  mutate(path = file.path(output_dir, paste0(file, ".png")))

pwalk(time_series_plots, \(path, plot, width, height, ...)
  ggsave(path, plot, width = width, height = height, dpi = 300, units = "cm"))
```

The tabs show the saved PNG files.

::: panel-tabset
```{r}
#| label: time-series-plots-tabs
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

for (i in seq_len(nrow(time_series_plots))) {
  cat("\n\n### ", time_series_plots$title[i], "\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("![](", time_series_plots$path[i], "){width=100%}\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

## 11) Annual summary tables

Create annual summary tables for each example scenario using the `make_annual_summary` function, which calculates annual totals for flow quantities and patient-days. Years are counted from the end of the burn-in (year 1 is the first year of the analysis period); the burn-in is excluded. Combine the annual summaries into a single data frame and save it as a CSV (`annual_summary_all.csv`, every year of the analysis period). As every scenario has stabilised before the end of the burn-in, each year of the analysis period is the same, so the table shows year 1 only. Hospital-acquired CDI cases (`annual_hospital_attributable_I`, estimated) are hospital-onset CDI cases (`annual_infected_in_hospital`) × the share of colonisations in the year that were acquired in hospital, as in the research question outcomes (Outcome B2).

```{r}
#| label: annual-summary-tables

annual_summary_all <- bind_rows(Map(make_annual_summary, scenario_post, names(scenario_post)))
write_csv(annual_summary_all,
          file.path(output_dir, "annual_summary_all.csv"))
knitr::kable(annual_summary_all |> filter(year == 1),
             caption = "Annual summary, year 1 of the analysis period, example scenarios")
```

## 12) Plots of annual summaries

Stacked bar plots of annual totals over the analysis period after the burn-in, for the example scenarios, grouped by setting of daily probability of testing and sensitivity (in the order set in `example_settings`), with P1, P2 and P3 side by side within each group:

- **Incident CDI cases by origin**: admitted with CDI, hospital-onset CDI in patients admitted colonised, and hospital-acquired CDI (estimated, as in Outcome B2). The top of each stack is all incident CDI cases.
- **Colonisations by source**: hospital-acquired colonisations from background acquisition (`beta0`) and from patient-to-patient transmission (secondary colonisations) from each state (C, I, Xtest, FN, Xtreat, and the transfer states T1, T3 and T4, each shown in a lighter shade next to the state it belongs to). These are colonisations, not CDI cases. For modelling simplicity, the background acquisition rate does not depend on the number of patients in each state.
- **Faecal specimens tested**: first tests and retests of false negatives.
- **Confirmed cases**: confirmed via first test and via retest (apportioned post hoc by the share of all tests that were retests).
- **Missed cases**: untested (discharged or died in I) and false negatives (discharged or died in FN, or in T4 awaiting return to the ward).
- **Outcomes of CDI cases**: discharged untreated, shown separately for untested patients (from I) and patients with a false negative result (from FN or T4), recovered after treatment (returned to a general ward or discharged from Xtreat) and died following CDI.
- **Bed-days by bed type**: patient bed-days per year in general ward beds and in side rooms (suspected cases, isolated under P3 only, and confirmed cases, isolated under P2 and P3, combined, including patients awaiting transfer out of a side room: T2 under P2, T4 and T5 under P3). The top of each stack is total patient bed-days; divide by 365 for the average number of occupied beds.

```{r}
#| label: annual-summaries-plots

annual_plots <- tribble(
  ~file,                          ~title,                     ~plot,
  "plot_cdi_cases_by_origin",     "CDI cases by origin",      plot_cdi_cases_by_origin_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_colonisations_by_source", "Colonisations by source",  plot_colonisation_sources_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_testing_bar",             "Faecal specimens tested",  plot_testing_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_case_confirmation_bar",   "Confirmed cases",          plot_case_confirmation_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_missed_cases_bar",        "Missed cases",             plot_missed_cases_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_case_outcomes_bar",       "Outcomes of CDI cases",    plot_case_outcomes_bar(example_annual_outcomes),
  "plot_bed_days_bar",            "Bed-days by bed type",     plot_bed_days_bar(example_annual_bed_days)
) |>
  mutate(path = file.path(output_dir, paste0(file, ".png")))

pwalk(annual_plots, \(path, plot, ...)
  ggsave(path, plot, width = 24, height = 13, dpi = 300, units = "cm"))
```

## 13) Table of research question outcomes

Sections [13) Table of research question outcomes] to [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity] present the results for the write-up (sections [10) Time-series plots up to stabilisation] to [12) Plots of annual summaries] are verification checks on the example scenarios).

**Research question outcomes table**

The table shows the outcomes of interest for the example scenarios, numbered as above, as annual totals after the burn-in, followed by the model outcomes required for the ICER numerator and denominator. Notes:

- The proportions of incident CDI cases confirmed (Outcome A5) and missed (Outcome A2) do not sum to 1: the gap is mainly deaths while awaiting a test result (tested, but neither confirmed nor missed).
- Differences in prevalence (Outcome B3) are discharge minus admission prevalence in percentage points (pp); a positive value indicates the hospital is a net source.
- CDI-attributable deaths (Outcome D4) are deaths following CDI that would not have occurred at the baseline death rate: deaths of untreated CDI patients (I, Xtest, FN, and T1, T3 and T4 awaiting transfer) × (1 − 1/`mortI_mult`) plus deaths of treated patients (Xtreat) × (1 − 1/`mortXtreat_mult`). Recovered patients awaiting transfer (T2, T5) die at the baseline rate and are not CDI deaths.
- Specimens tested per confirmed case (Outcome C6) is shown as "-" where no cases are confirmed (no testing or 0% sensitivity).
- Mean times from CDI symptom onset (entry to I) to first test (Outcome D5, entry to Xtest, when the specimen is taken) and to treatment (Outcome D6, entry to Xtreat) are among the cases that get there before discharge or death. They are calculated exactly from the scenario's rates (`mean_wait_to_state()`), and include waits for transfer to a side room (T3 under P3 before the test, T1 under P2 before treatment), the test turnaround and, for treatment, any false negative results and retests.

The effect of the isolation policies across the daily probability of testing and test sensitivity is shown in section [14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity], and the change in outcomes from improving test sensitivity, for each policy, in section [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity].

Final cumulative outcomes for every scenario in the grid (totals over the `r analysis_years`-year analysis period after the burn-in) are saved as CSVs:

- `final_outcomes_all.csv`: all cumulative outcomes from `make_final_outcomes`, joined to the control values and patient-days, with the derived outcomes (proportions, prevalence differences, specimens per confirmed case)
- `research_outcomes_all.csv`: the research question outcomes table (below), per year, for every scenario
- `grid_key_outcomes.csv` and `grid_key_outcome_differences.csv`: the outcomes compared in sections [14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity] and [15) Plots of change in outcomes due to increasing test sensitivity] (counts as annual totals), and their differences between policies, in long format
- `grid_rates.csv`: rates per 10,000 patient bed-days (CDI, hospital-onset CDI, hospital-acquired CDI, faecal specimens tested), the proportion of patient bed-days in a side room, the proportion of CDI cases missed, and missed cases per year by origin, for every scenario, in long format

```{r}
#| label: research-questions-outcomes-table

write_csv(grid_results, file.path(output_dir, "final_outcomes_all.csv"))
write_csv(grid_long,    file.path(output_dir, "grid_key_outcomes.csv"))
write_csv(grid_diffs,   file.path(output_dir, "grid_key_outcome_differences.csv"))
write_csv(make_grid_rates(grid_results, analysis_years) |>
            make_grid_outcomes_long(spec = rate_spec),
          file.path(output_dir, "grid_rates.csv"))

# Research question outcomes, per year
research_outcomes <- make_research_outcomes_table(example_annual_outcomes, example_annual_bed_days,
                                                  per_year = TRUE)
write_csv(research_outcomes, file.path(output_dir, "research_outcomes.csv"))
write_csv(make_research_outcomes_table(annualise(final_outcomes), annualise(grid_runs$patient_days),
                                       per_year = TRUE),
          file.path(output_dir, "research_outcomes_all.csv"))
knitr::kable(research_outcomes, caption = "Research question outcomes and ICER inputs per year after the burn-in, example scenarios")
```

**Testing outputs by daily probability of testing.** The daily probability that an untested CDI case is sent for testing (`prob_test_daily`) sets the case identification rate, `gamma = -log(1 - prob_test_daily)`. Identification competes with discharge and death from I, so the table shows what follows from each value:

- **Mean time to testing if not discharged or dead first (days)**: `1 / gamma`.
- **Actual mean time to testing among cases tested (days)**: `1 / (gamma + disI + mortI)`, shorter than `1 / gamma` because discharge and death cut off the longer waits. It is the same under every policy (under P3 the specimen is taken after the move to a side room, a mean of `r fixed$t_patient_transfer` days later; Outcome D5 includes this).
- **Incident CDI cases ever sent for testing (%)**: suspected cases identified / incident CDI cases, which equals `gamma / (gamma + disI + mortI)` at steady state (shown for P1; under P3 a few die in T3 before their first test).
- **Prevalent CDI cases ever tested at model stabilisation (Outcome A4)**, under each policy: the share of CDI patient-days spent in a tested state, averaged over the analysis period. The specimen is taken on entry to Xtest, so the tested states are Xtest, FN, Xtreat, T1 and T4, plus the share of T3 (awaiting a side room under P3) that came from FN; patients in I, and those in T3 who came from I, have not yet been tested. T3 is not split by origin, so its share from FN is estimated from the inflows to T3 (exact at steady state). Outcome A4 is higher than the incident share because tested cases stay in hospital longer, and it also depends on the policy and test sensitivity. For comparison, Mawer et al. (2019) found 33% of hospital-onset diarrhoea patients in hospital had ever been tested for CDI (a different denominator: all diarrhoea, not CDI).

The table is at the test sensitivity set below, and is saved as `testing_outputs.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: testing-outputs-table
testing_outputs_sens <- 0.5   # must be a value in the test_sens vector

# Rate of leaving I by discharge or death (the same under every policy), for the actual mean time to
# testing among cases tested
exit_rate_I <- grid_runs$parms$disI[1] + grid_runs$parms$mortI[1]

testing_outputs <- make_testing_outputs(grid_results, exit_rate_I, testing_outputs_sens)
write_csv(testing_outputs, file.path(output_dir, "testing_outputs.csv"))

knitr::kable(
  format_testing_outputs(testing_outputs),
  caption = paste0("Testing outputs by daily probability of testing, at ",
                   scales::percent(testing_outputs_sens), " test sensitivity (Outcome A4: prevalent CDI cases ever ",
                   "tested at model stabilisation, by isolation policy)")
)
```

## 14) Plots of outcomes by daily probability of testing and test sensitivity

Compare the three isolation policies across every combination of daily probability of testing and test sensitivity in the grid, for every research question outcome, Outcome A1 to Outcome D6 (set by the `plot` column of `grid_outcome_spec` in `Scripts/Model4_Functions.R`), apart from the colonisation and CDI prevalence at admission (Outcome B3; fixed inputs, the same in every scenario) and confirmed cases started on treatment (Outcome C7; equal to Outcome A5). Counts are annual totals over the analysis period (the `r analysis_years`-year total after a `r burn_in`-day burn-in, divided by `r analysis_years`); proportions, prevalence differences, length of stay and mean times are over the whole analysis period. All values are also saved in `final_outcomes_all.csv`.

**Note on total and hospital-acquired CDI cases.** Differences in total CDI cases (Outcome A1) between scenarios are driven entirely by differences in hospital-acquired CDI cases (Outcome B2), so the difference plots for Outcome A1 and Outcome B2 are identical. Admissions arrive at a fixed rate, so patients admitted with CDI (`r scales::comma(round(grid_results_annual$cum_admitted_infected[1]))` per year) and patients admitted colonised are the same in every scenario. Testing and isolation act only on infected patients, so they do not change how colonised patients progress, lose colonisation or leave hospital, and progressions to CDI among patients admitted colonised are also the same in every scenario (`r scales::comma(round(grid_results_annual$cum_infected_in_hospital[1] - grid_results_annual$cum_hospital_attributable_I[1]))` per year). Total and hospital-onset CDI cases therefore differ from hospital-acquired CDI cases by a constant.

Each tab shows one outcome, as:

1.  **Line plot**: outcome against test sensitivity, with one line for each daily probability of testing in `grid_line_sent` (by default 0.00 (no testing), 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.40), and the same y axis for each isolation policy.
2.  **Differences from P1**: the same, for P2 minus P1 and P3 minus P1 at the same daily probability of testing and test sensitivity, placed under P2 and P3 in the line plot above (the space under P1 is left empty). A negative value means less of the outcome than with no isolation. This shows the effect of each isolation policy more clearly than the totals, which are dominated by the differences across the daily probability of testing.
3.  **Heatmaps**: test sensitivity (x) by daily probability of testing (y, one row per grid value, evenly spaced although the values are not, from no testing at the bottom to the most testing at the top), for every grid value. The top row shows the outcome under each policy, with one colour scale shared across the policies (yellow lowest, purple highest). The bottom row shows the differences P2 minus P1 and P3 minus P1, under P2 and P3 (the space under P1 is left empty), with one colour scale shared across both (yellow largest negative difference, purple largest positive difference).

Differences between policies, including P3 vs P2 (the incremental effect of also isolating suspected cases), are saved in `grid_key_outcome_differences.csv`.

With no testing, no patients are tested, so test sensitivity has no effect and the line is flat. The mean times to first test and to treatment (Outcome D5, Outcome D6) have no value with no testing (and Outcome D6 none at 0% sensitivity); those heatmap tiles are grey.

**Note on very low test sensitivity.** At low sensitivity (roughly 10% or below), testing can increase CDI, hospital-acquired CDI, missed cases and deaths compared with no testing. Most tested patients receive a false negative result and return to the general ward (FN), where they continue to transmit at `betaI`. They are retested after `t_wait_retest` days, which is sooner than the typical time to discharge, so many cycle repeatedly between FN and awaiting a result (Xtest). There is no discharge from Xtest, so each retest also keeps them in hospital for longer. These patients are held back from treatment (and, for confirmed cases, isolation), and are kept infectious in hospital for longer than untested patients. This is intended: it shows the effect of testing with a low-sensitivity assay.

```{r}
#| label: note-values
#| include: false
# Helpers for the figures quoted in the notes in sections 14 and 15 (calculated from the grid as
# annual totals, so they stay correct if parameters change)
P1 <- "none"; P2 <- "confirmed"; P3 <- "suspected_and_confirmed"
# Highest daily probability of testing in the grid (the most testing), used for the figures below
max_sent <- max(grid_results$prob_test_daily)
# Section 15: the change from increasing test sensitivity from sens_from to sens_to (both must be values
# in test_sens), and the daily probabilities of testing shown in its tables (must be values in
# prob_test_daily)
sens_from <- 0.5
sens_to   <- 0.8
gain_table_sent <- c(0.03, 0.40)
on_grid <- function(df, pol, sent, sens) {
  df$isolation_policy == pol & abs(df$prob_test_daily - sent) < 1e-6 & abs(df$test_sens - sens) < 1e-6
}
# Annual value of a final outcome column for one scenario
gval <- function(var, pol, sent, sens) grid_results_annual[[var]][on_grid(grid_results_annual, pol, sent, sens)]
# Share of test results that are positive, theta / (theta + pi) (deaths while awaiting a result give no
# result, so are not counted)
pos_share <- function(pol, sens, sent = max_sent) {
  p <- grid_runs$parms[on_grid(grid_runs$parms, pol, sent, sens), ]
  p$theta / (p$theta + p$pi)
}
n0 <- function(x) scales::comma(round(x))
n0p <- function(x) scales::comma(round(x), style_positive = "plus")
# Formats: pc for test sensitivity (%), prob for probabilities (decimal, e.g. 0.40)
pc <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
prob <- fmt_prob

# Missed CDI cases per year at the highest daily probability of testing: P3 minus P1 by sensitivity
miss_gap <- tibble(sens = sort(unique(grid_results$test_sens))) |>
  mutate(gap = map_dbl(sens, \(s) gval("cum_total_missed_cases", P3, max_sent, s) -
                                  gval("cum_total_missed_cases", P1, max_sent, s)))
miss_trough_sens <- miss_gap$sens[which.min(miss_gap$gap)]
# Lowest sensitivity at which P3 has more missed cases than P1 (NA if it never does)
miss_cross_sens  <- if (any(miss_gap$gap > 0)) min(miss_gap$sens[miss_gap$gap > 0]) else NA_real_
```

**Note on differences between isolation policies at low test sensitivity.** With no testing, nobody is identified as a suspected case, so no patients reach Xtest or Xtreat and the three policies give identical results. With testing and low sensitivity, there are more CDI cases (and hospital-acquired CDI and colonisations) under P1 and P2 than under P3. This is not because infected patients stay longer in I: identified patients leave I sooner than without testing (I patient-days fall sharply). The extra transmission happens after they leave I, while they cycle between awaiting a result (Xtest) and false negatives on the ward (FN):

- Under P1 and P2, suspected cases wait for their result on a general ward and transmit at the full `betaI`. Under P3 they wait in a side room and transmit at `betaI * beta_mult_isolated`. With repeated retesting, patients spend many days in Xtest, so this difference drives most of the gap: at a daily probability of testing of `r prob(max_sent)` and 0% sensitivity, colonisations from Xtest are about `r n0(signif(gval("cum_colonised_from_Xtest", P1, max_sent, 0), 2))` per year under P1 and P2 and about `r n0(signif(gval("cum_colonised_from_Xtest", P3, max_sent, 0), 2))` under P3.
- From about 10% sensitivity, some cases are confirmed. P1 is then higher than P2, because confirmed cases (Xtreat) are treated on a general ward and transmit at `betaXtreat` rather than `betaXtreat * beta_mult_isolated`.

**Note on missed CDI cases** (tab Outcome A2, Missed CDI cases). The figures below are per year, at a daily probability of testing of `r prob(max_sent)`; see also the note on missed cases in the introduction.

- **Line plot: more missed cases under P1 and P2 at low sensitivity.** At low sensitivity most missed cases are false negatives, and P1 and P2 have more than P3 because there are more CDI cases to miss, as suspected cases wait for their result on a general ward (see the note above): at 0% sensitivity, there are `r n0(gval("cum_total_infected_incidence", P1, max_sent, 0) - gval("cum_total_infected_incidence", P3, max_sent, 0))` more CDI cases per year under P1 and P2 than under P3. The share of results that are positive is the same under every policy (equal to the test sensitivity; see the note on test sensitivity in the introduction).
- **Line plot: P3 compared with P1 at high sensitivity.** `r if (is.na(miss_cross_sens)) "P3 has fewer missed cases than P1 at every test sensitivity. The share of CDI cases missed untested (discharged or dying in I, plus the few dying in T3 under P3) is almost the same under every policy, as transfer time is not added to the case identification rate, so P3 keeps the advantage of fewer CDI cases even when false negatives are rare." else paste0("From ", pc(miss_cross_sens), " sensitivity, P3 has more missed cases than P1, as false negatives become rare.")`
- **The difference plots.** The P3 vs P1 difference is most negative at `r pc(miss_trough_sens)` sensitivity (`r n0p(min(miss_gap$gap))` per year). As sensitivity rises, all three policies confirm more cases, the pool of false negatives shrinks for everyone and the differences narrow (`r n0p(miss_gap$gap[which.max(miss_gap$sens)])` per year at `r pc(max(miss_gap$sens))` sensitivity). With no testing nobody is tested, so the differences are zero.

```{r}

tab_outcomes <- grid_outcome_spec |>
  filter(plot) |>
  mutate(
    lines        = file.path(output_dir, paste0("grid_lines_", variable, ".png")),
    diff_lines   = file.path(output_dir, paste0("grid_lines_diff_", variable, ".png")),
```
